content: The prioritization process of a country aims to enhance the existing monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework. This process involves a tiered set of indicators: 1. National Core Indicators: This is a set of 15 indicators that represent the fundamental metrics for tracking progress against the targets of a national strategy. These indicators are broadly applicable across various country contexts. 2. National Priority Indicators (Top 40): This set includes the 15 national core indicators plus an additional 25 indicators, making a total of 40. These indicators provide real-time data to program managers, enabling them to improve services. They are designed to be feasible for collection within the constraints of current data collection systems. The additional 25 indicators are particularly relevant for addressing immediate or short-term challenges in scaling up services or overcoming barriers in service delivery. As national programs evolve or respond to new developments in the epidemic or implementation environment, some of these indicators may be replaced with others. 3. Differentiated Use: The guideline also recommends a tailored set of indicators for countries with specific epidemiological characteristics, such as a high burden of co-morbidities like tuberculosis (TB) and HIV, or unique programmatic needs, such as increasing injection safety or scaling up voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC). 4. Impact and Burden Indicators: These are modeled indicators that complement the program-based Top 40. They are essential for quantifying changes in the epidemic and assessing the effectiveness of the response. Key Updates in the Guideline: The guideline introduces an updated set of core indicators aligned with those of partner organizations. It adopts a differentiated approach for countries to prioritize and select indicators. The recommended indicators reflect the latest technical guidelines for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), prevention for adolescent girls and young women, HIV testing, antiretroviral treatment (ART), viral load monitoring, TB/HIV integration, and the elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT). The guideline emphasizes the use of 15 core and 40 priority national indicators to strengthen program data utilization. It provides guidance on conducting regular data reviews to identify gaps in the cascade of services, from prevention and testing to treatment, viral suppression, and management of co-morbidities. Enhanced digital content is included, along with an accelerator kit to ensure that WHO’s technical recommendations are accurately integrated into the digital systems adopted by countries. Development Process: The updated guidelines were developed by WHO staff and consultants through a review of recent global and regional guidance documents, consultative meetings, and input from technical experts. The indicators were identified in collaboration with experts from country-level, regional, and global perspectives. Virtual working groups, comprising representatives from ministries of health, non-governmental organizations, academic institutions, and development partners, prioritized and organized the indicators. Most indicators were modified to align with interim partner guidance and technical recommendations, while some were retired. The guidelines aim to align with other M&E frameworks, such as UNAIDS’ Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) and the Global Fund’s Modular Framework. Intended Audience: The guideline is primarily designed for HIV program staff and partners involved in the collection, analysis, and use of HIV-related strategic information at all levels of the health sector. This includes national-level staff responsible for establishing strategic information policies, guidelines, frameworks, and tools, as well as those involved in data collection and analysis at subnational and service delivery levels. Other potential users include stakeholders from non-governmental organizations, private-sector care providers, civil society, and academic groups engaged in teaching and research. These stakeholders can participate in government-led consultative processes for designing or redesigning strategic information systems. Organization of the Document: The document is divided into three parts: 1. Part 1: Strategic Information – A Consolidated Framework: This section provides the rationale for using strategic information to monitor and manage the health sector response to the HIV epidemic. It contextualizes the guidance within the global strategy for ending AIDS. 2. Part 2: Strong SI Systems for Effective Decision-Making: This section focuses on selecting and prioritizing country-specific indicator sets. It explains the rationale for choosing national core and priority indicators and offers considerations for adapting the recommended sets to different country contexts. It also outlines the key components of a robust strategic information system built around these indicators. 3. Part 3: Recommended Indicators – National Core and Priority: This section provides detailed information about the recommended indicators, organized by program area. It includes definitions, data sources, measurement approaches, and references to additional materials for operationalizing the collection and use of indicator data. Strategic Framework: The guideline focuses on two primary objectives of strategic information: Program Monitoring: Ensuring accountability for the 95–95–95 targets and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Program Management: Analyzing and using routine disaggregated cascade data to improve service delivery and quality. The health sector response to HIV is monitored through a coherent results chain of key inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impacts. The recommended indicators span the entire results chain but emphasize tracking outputs related to coverage and quality, as well as key programmatic and clinical outcomes. HIV Cascade of Services: The critical outputs and outcomes of the health sector response to HIV can be visualized through a cascade of services anchored by the 95–95–95 targets for 2030. The cascade format highlights gaps in service coverage and quality, providing insights into patient follow-up and coordination between service areas. Regular cascade data reviews are promoted to identify gaps and improve program management. Routine Data Reviews: Strategic information provides managers with essential data to improve services. Regular analysis of these data helps identify problems and areas for focus. The guideline supports the practice of routine data reviews, supplemented periodically with data from models and surveys, to enhance decision-making and program improvement.
